subject: paediatrics
title: Pediatric Leukemias and Renal Neoplasms: ALL, AML, and Wilms Tumour

steps.tx: Clonal proliferation and marrow replacement by immature lymphoid progenitor blast cells represents the most common childhood malignancy. Peak incidence of **pediatric acute lymphoblastic leukaemia** (ALL) occurs between two and five years of age, with precursor B-cell ALL accounting for eighty-five percent. Marrow infiltration suppresses normal hematopoiesis, causing pallor, petechiae, refractory fever, generalized lymphadenopathy, and bone pain from leukemic periosteal expansion.
steps.say: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia is the most common childhood cancer, peaking between two and five years. Bone marrow replacement causes pallor, purpura, fever, and bone pain.

vis.alt: Peripheral blood smear and marrow aspirate showing high nucleocytoplasmic ratio lymphoblasts in acute lymphoblastic leukemia.
vis.caption: Marrow aspirate displaying dense replacement by immature lymphoblasts with high nucleocytoplasmic ratio in ALL. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Bone marrow aspiration and multiparametric flow cytometry establish the definitive diagnosis and lineage immunophenotyping. Confirming acute leukemia requires demonstrating **marrow lymphoblasts exceeding twenty percent** on morphological examination of bone marrow aspirates. Precursor B-cell ALL is characterized by positive expression of CD19, CD10 (common ALL antigen CALLA), CD22, and terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT), while lacking myeloperoxidase.
steps.say: Demonstrating more than twenty percent lymphoblasts in the bone marrow establishes the diagnosis. B-ALL blasts express CD19, CD10, and terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase.

rows: Small to medium blasts, high N:C ratio
Variable size; prominent anterior mediastinal mass
Large blasts, abundant cytoplasm, Auer rods

steps.tx: Multidrug risk-stratified chemotherapy protocols cure over ninety percent of children with acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Modern therapy for **pediatric ALL chemotherapy phases** comprises four successive stages: four-drug induction (vincristine, corticosteroid, L-asparaginase, and daunorubicin) achieving complete remission in ninety-eight percent, followed by consolidation/intensification, central nervous system-directed intrathecal therapy, and continuation maintenance for two to three years.
steps.say: Four-drug induction chemotherapy achieves complete remission in ninety-eight percent of children with ALL. Total therapy lasts two to three years, including maintenance methotrexate.

left.title: Treatment Phase Sequences
points: Induction: 4 weeks to induce complete morphological remission
Consolidation / Intensification: eradicates residual disease
CNS prophylaxis: intrathecal methotrexate (no cranial RT)
Maintenance: oral 6-mercaptopurine daily + methotrexate weekly

right.title: Minimal Residual Disease (MRD)
points: Measured by flow cytometry or PCR at end of induction
MRD <0.01% (<1 blast per 10,000 cells) defines deep remission
Most powerful independent prognostic predictor
High MRD prompts treatment escalation to HSCT

steps.tx: Myeloid blast proliferation in childhood acute myeloid leukemia requires aggressive myeloablative therapy and intensive supportive care. Accounting for fifteen percent of pediatric leukemias, **pediatric acute myeloid leukemia** (AML) presents with life-threatening complications including severe disseminated intravascular coagulation in acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL with t(15;17)), chloromas (extramedullary granulocytic sarcomas), and gum hypertrophy, showing Auer rods on cytology.
steps.say: Acute myeloid leukemia features Auer rods, gum hypertrophy, and chloromas. Acute promyelocytic leukemia with t(15;17) carries a high risk of fatal DIC.

rows: Severe consumption DIC with fatal haemorrhage
Greenish orbital tumor, skin nodules, spinal mass

steps.tx: The most common primary malignant renal tumor of childhood arises from primitive metanephric blastema. Typically presenting between two and five years of age, **Wilms tumour or nephroblastoma** manifests in ninety percent as an asymptomatic, smooth, firm, non-tender abdominal flank mass that rarely crosses the midline. Microscopic examination demonstrates classic triphasic histology consisting of blastemal, epithelial, and stromal mesenchymal elements.
steps.say: Wilms tumour is the commonest pediatric renal malignancy, presenting as a firm flank mass that does not cross the midline. Histology is classically triphasic.

vis.alt: Diagram displaying congenital syndromic associations of Wilms tumor including WAGR and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndromes.
vis.caption: Congenital syndromic associations linking chromosome 11p WT1 deletions to Wilms tumor and aniridia. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Specific congenital malformation syndromes and genetic deletions dramatically increase the risk of nephroblastoma. Arising from deletions of the WT1 tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 11p13, **WAGR syndrome and Wilms tumour** comprises Wilms tumor, sporadic aniridia, genitourinary anomalies (cryptorchidism, ambiguous genitalia), and intellectual disability. Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (11p15 WT2 overgrowth) features hemihypertrophy, macroglossia, and omphalocele.
steps.say: WAGR syndrome links 11p13 WT1 deletion to Wilms tumor, aniridia, and genital anomalies. Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome features hemihypertrophy and macroglossia.

left.title: WAGR Syndrome (11p13 Deletion)
points: Wilms tumour: 50% lifetime risk
Aniridia: complete or partial absence of iris
Genitourinary anomalies (hypospadias, cryptorchidism)
Range of intellectual developmental delays

right.title: Beckwith-Wiedemann Syndrome
points: 11p15.5 imprinting anomaly (IGF2 overexpression)
Hemihypertrophy (asymmetric limb growth)
Macroglossia, omphalocele, neonatal hypoglycemia
Ultrasound surveillance every 3 months until age 8

steps.tx: Clinical and radiological differentiation distinguishes renal Wilms tumor from adrenal neuroblastoma reliably. On physical examination and contrast computed tomography, **Wilms tumour versus neuroblastoma** is characterized by a smooth, mobile flank mass that displaces rather than encases surrounding renal vessels, rarely crosses the abdominal midline, and exhibits a claw sign of parenchymal stretching, whereas neuroblastoma is nodular and calcified.
steps.say: Wilms tumor is smooth, rarely crosses the midline, and displaces vessels. Neuroblastoma is irregular, crosses the midline, encases major arteries, and shows dense calcifications.

rows: Encases and encrusts aorta and IVC
Normal urine VMA and HVA levels

steps.tx: Multimodal risk-adapted treatment combining surgical resection and chemotherapy achieves cure in ninety percent of children with Wilms tumor. Standard staging directs management: Stage I and II tumors confined to the kidney undergo **radical nephrectomy and adjuvant chemotherapy** with dactinomycin and vincristine. In tumors exhibiting diffuse anaplasia (TP53 mutations) or advanced Stage III and IV with pulmonary metastases, doxorubicin and flank radiotherapy are incorporated.
steps.say: Radical nephrectomy and vincristine with dactinomycin achieve ninety percent cure rates in Wilms tumor. Diffuse anaplasia indicates unfavorable histology requiring escalated therapy.

left.title: Histological Stratification
points: Favorable histology: classic triphasic without anaplasia
Excellent cure rates (>90% 5-year overall survival)
Unfavorable histology: diffuse nuclear anaplasia (TP53)
Higher relapse risk requiring intensified therapy

right.title: Surgical Principles in Nephrectomy
points: Transabdominal incision to inspect contralateral kidney
Early ligation of renal vein to prevent embolization
Meticulous handling to avoid intraoperative capsule rupture
Capsule spill upstages patient to Stage III, requiring RT
